Paul warns against another gospel (verses 1–4)

Paul wanted to protect the Corinthians from the corrupting influence of false apostles.

There is one Jesus, one Spirit and one gospel to be proclaimed and received.

Why should hostile schemers turn the Corinthians against the apostle who had first taught them the faith?

They should not listen to people who, without just reason, tried to draw them away from those God had used to bring them to conversion.

Paul served without using ministry for personal gain (verses 5–15)

It is far better to speak plainly while living openly and consistently with the gospel than to be admired by thousands and lifted up in pride.

A person admired as an impressive speaker may still disgrace the gospel through sinful attitudes and an unholy life.

Paul deliberately avoided giving his opponents any basis for accusing him of self-interested motives in preaching.

He would not let the false teachers in Corinth gain that advantage over him.

Hypocrisy is a real danger, particularly because Satan exerts considerable influence over people who continue living in disobedience.

But we must beware of an opposite temptation too.

Satan can advance his purposes by setting good works against Christ's atonement, as though salvation could be earned rather than received by faith and grace.

False workers will eventually be exposed, and their efforts will end in ruin.

Henry argues that Satan's servants can sometimes present the law alone or the gospel alone in misleading ways.

The test of a sound system is whether it teaches the law as rightly understood and upheld through faith in Christ's righteousness and atoning work, together with participation in his Spirit.

Paul explains why he must defend his integrity (verses 16–21)

Christians ought to humble themselves in obedience to the Lord's command and example.

Nevertheless, wisdom is needed to decide when it is appropriate to speak of things we have lawfully done.

That includes acknowledging what God has done for us, within us and through us.

Paul's defense was not merely boasting.

He referred to real behavior that exposed the character of the false apostles.

How astonishing that such people could bring their followers into bondage, take advantage of them and even insult them—and still retain their allegiance!

Paul's hardships as a minister of Christ (verses 22–33)

Paul recounted his work and suffering not from pride or love of applause, but to honor God, who had strengthened him for such service.

His experiences also revealed the difference between his ministry and the claims of opponents who tried to destroy his reputation and usefulness.

Consider the long record of dangers, deprivation, trouble and suffering!

And notice his patience, perseverance, diligence, cheerfulness and usefulness amid it all.

How little reason do we have to love this world's luxury and splendor when this blessed apostle experienced so much hardship while serving Christ.

Our hardest work and greatest sacrifices often seem small compared with Paul's.

Even our troubles may be scarcely noticeable beside his.

His example should lead us to examine whether we truly follow Christ.

Here we may learn patience, courage and steadfast trust in God.

Let us think less highly of ourselves.

Above all, let us speak strictly and consistently truthfully before God's presence, attributing everything to his glory as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, blessed forever.
classic_reading:
[2Cor.11.1-2Cor.11.4]
Chapter 11
Chapter Outline
The apostle gives the reasons for speaking in his own commendation. | (1-14) |
Shows that he had freely preached the gospel. | (5-15) |
Explains what he was going to add in defence of his own character. | (16-21) |
He gives an account of his labours, cares, sufferings, dangers, and deliverances. | (22-33) |
Verses 1-4
The apostle desired to preserve the Corinthians from being corrupted by the false apostles. There is but one Jesus, one Spirit, and one gospel, to be preached to them, and received by them; and why should any be prejudiced, by the devices of an adversary, against him who first taught them in faith? They should not listen to men, who, without cause, would draw them away from those who were the means of their conversion.
[2Cor.11.5-2Cor.11.15]
Verses 5-15
It is far better to be plain in speech, yet walking openly and consistently with the gospel, than to be admired by thousands, and be lifted up in pride, so as to disgrace the gospel by evil tempers and unholy lives. The apostle would not give room for any to accuse him of worldly designs in preaching the gospel, that others who opposed him at Corinth, might not in this respect gain advantage against him. Hypocrisy may be looked for, especially when we consider the great power which Satan, who rules in the hearts of the children of disobedience, has upon the minds of many. And as there are temptations to evil conduct, so there is equal danger on the other side. It serves Satan's purposes as well, to set up good works against the atonement of Christ, and salvation by faith and grace. But the end will discover those who are deceitful workers; their work will end in ruin. Satan will allow his ministers to preach either the law or the gospel separately; but the law as established by faith in Christ's righteousness and atonement, and the partaking of his Spirit, is the test of every false system.
[2Cor.11.16-2Cor.11.21]
Verses 16-21
It is the duty and practice of Christians to humble themselves, in obedience to the command and example of the Lord; yet prudence must direct in what it is needful to do things which we may do lawfully, even the speaking of what God has wrought for us, and in us, and by us. Doubtless here is reference to facts in which the character of the false apostles had been shown. It is astonishing to see how such men bring their followers into bondage, and how they take from them and insult them.
[2Cor.11.22-2Cor.11.33]
Verses 22-33
The apostle gives an account of his labours and sufferings; not out of pride or vain-glory, but to the honour of God, who enabled him to do and suffer so much for the cause of Christ; and shows wherein he excelled the false apostles, who tried to lessen his character and usefulness. It astonishes us to reflect on this account of his dangers, hardships, and sufferings, and to observe his patience, perseverance, diligence, cheerfulness, and usefulness, in the midst of all these trials. See what little reason we have to love the pomp and plenty of this world, when this blessed apostle felt so much hardship in it. Our utmost diligence and services appear unworthy of notice when compared with his, and our difficulties and trials scarcely can be perceived. It may well lead us to inquire whether or not we really are followers of Christ. Here we may study patience, courage, and firm trust in God. Here we may learn to think less of ourselves; and we should ever strictly keep to truth, as in God's presence; and should refer all to his glory, as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed for evermore.

Paul's heavenly revelations (verses 1–6)

There is no serious doubt that Paul was speaking about himself.

He did not know exactly how his experience had occurred.

Perhaps heavenly realities were shown to him while his body remained in a trance, as had sometimes happened to earlier prophets.

Perhaps his soul was temporarily separated from his body and taken into heaven.

Or perhaps both his body and soul were caught up together.

Paul himself did not know, and Henry does not pretend to resolve the matter.

We are neither capable of understanding nor meant to know every detail of heaven's glorious life at present.

Paul did not try to publish a description of everything he heard.

Instead, he proclaimed the teaching of Jesus Christ.

That teaching is the foundation upon which the church rests and upon which our faith and hope must be built.

The vision should enlarge our expectations of future glory, but it should also make us content with the ordinary means God has provided for learning his truth and will.

The thorn in the flesh and sufficient grace (verses 7–10)

Paul explained how God kept him humble after receiving extraordinary visions and revelations.

The Lord allowed a thorn in the flesh so that Paul would not become proud.

Scripture does not tell us what this thorn was.

Henry leaves open whether it was a severe outward trouble or a powerful temptation.

God can turn even the reproaches of enemies to good by using them to expose and restrain our pride.

When God loves us, he will not leave us to become proud beyond measure.

Spiritual burdens may be used to cure spiritual pride.

Paul called the thorn a messenger of Satan.

Satan meant it for evil, but God overruled it for good.

Prayer is a remedy for every wound and a source of help in every illness or trial.

When we face thorns in the flesh, we should devote ourselves to prayer.

If an answer is not given at the first or second request, we should continue praying.

Troubles teach us to pray. Troubles that remain can teach us perseverance in prayer.

God accepts the prayers of faith, but he does not always grant what we ask.

Sometimes he grants a request in judgment; at other times he refuses a request in love.

If he does not remove our trouble or temptation but gives us sufficient grace, we have no reason to complain.

Grace includes God's gracious favor toward us.

It is enough to illuminate and strengthen our souls, sustain our life and comfort us amid suffering.

God's strength is made perfect in human weakness.

Our weakness becomes the occasion for his grace to appear even more clearly.

When we know we are weak in ourselves, we are moved to Christ for strength and enjoy the supply he gives.

Paul defends his concern for the Corinthians (verses 11–21)

We should defend the good reputation of faithful people when that reputation is unfairly attacked.

We owe particular gratitude to those whom God has used to bring spiritual blessings into our lives.

Paul's words demonstrate the character and intentions of a faithful gospel minister.

His chief aim was to do good.

He expressed concern that on his next visit he might find professing believers living in sins that required painful correction.

Even the failings of those under their care can deeply humble faithful ministers.

God may use those disappointments to humble ministers who would otherwise be tempted by pride.

The Corinthians' behavior showed how far the false teachers had drawn their followers away from godliness.

How grievous that such sins can be found among people professing the gospel!

Yet this happened even during the apostles' own lives and has happened far too often since.
classic_reading:
[2Cor.12.1-2Cor.12.6]
Chapter 12
Chapter Outline
The apostle's revelations. | (1-6) |
Which were improved to his spiritual advantage. | (7-10) |
The signs of an apostle were in him, His purpose of making them a visit; but he expresses his fear lest he should have to be severe with some. | (11-21) |
Verses 1-6
There can be no doubt the apostle speaks of himself. Whether heavenly things were brought down to him, while his body was in a trance, as in the case of ancient prophets; or whether his soul was dislodged from the body for a time, and taken up into heaven, or whether he was taken up, body and soul together, he knew not. We are not capable, nor is it fit we should yet know, the particulars of that glorious place and state. He did not attempt to publish to the world what he had heard there, but he set forth the doctrine of Christ. On that foundation the church is built, and on that we must build our faith and hope. And while this teaches us to enlarge our expectations of the glory that shall be revealed, it should render us contented with the usual methods of learning the truth and will of God.
[2Cor.12.7-2Cor.12.10]
Verses 7-10
The apostle gives an account of the method God took to keep him humble, and to prevent his being lifted up above measure, on account of the visions and revelations he had. We are not told what this thorn in the flesh was, whether some great trouble, or some great temptation. But God often brings this good out of evil, that the reproaches of our enemies help to hide pride from us. If God loves us, he will keep us from being exalted above measure; and spiritual burdens are ordered to cure spiritual pride. This thorn in the flesh is said to be a messenger of Satan which he sent for evil; but God designed it, and overruled it for good. Prayer is a salve for every sore, a remedy for every malady; and when we are afflicted with thorns in the flesh, we should give ourselves to prayer. If an answer be not given to the first prayer, nor to the second, we are to continue praying. Troubles are sent to teach us to pray; and are continued, to teach us to continue instant in prayer. Though God accepts the prayer of faith, yet he does not always give what is asked for: as he sometimes grants in wrath, so he sometimes denies in love. When God does not take away our troubles and temptations, yet, if he gives grace enough for us, we have no reason to complain. Grace signifies the good-will of God towards us, and that is enough to enlighten and enliven us, sufficient to strengthen and comfort in all afflictions and distresses. His strength is made perfect in our weakness. Thus his grace is manifested and magnified. When we are weak in ourselves, then we are strong in the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ; when we feel that we are weak in ourselves, then we go to Christ, receive strength from him, and enjoy most the supplies of Divine strength and grace.
[2Cor.12.11-2Cor.12.21]
Verses 11-21
We owe it to good men, to stand up in the defence of their reputation; and we are under special obligations to those from whom we have received benefit, especially spiritual benefit, to own them as instruments in God's hand of good to us. Here is an account of the apostle's behaviour and kind intentions; in which see the character of a faithful minister of the gospel. This was his great aim and design, to do good. Here are noticed several sins commonly found among professors of religion. Falls and misdeeds are humbling to a minister; and God sometimes takes this way to humble those who might be tempted to be lifted up. These vast verses show to what excesses the false teachers had drawn aside their deluded followers. How grievous it is that such evils should be found among professors of the gospel! Yet thus it is, and has been too often, and it was so even in the days of the apostles.

A warning and an examination of genuine faith (verses 1–6)

The Lord patiently bears with sinners because he is gracious.

But his patience does not mean that he will never judge.

Those who remain obstinate and refuse to repent will eventually meet the judgment they have resisted.

At the crucifixion, Jesus appeared weak and helpless to the world.

But his resurrection and living power revealed that he was truly divine.

Similarly, the apostles often appeared insignificant and contemptible in human eyes.

Yet God used them as instruments through which his power became evident.

Paul called the Corinthians to examine themselves.

They should test their attitudes, conduct and spiritual experience as gold is tested with a touchstone.

If they could see genuine evidence that Christ had accepted them, they ought also to recognize the authenticity of Paul's apostolic service.

We should examine whether Jesus Christ lives in us.

His presence is known through the Holy Spirit's work, the graces he produces and the establishing of Christ's kingdom in our hearts.

Let us question our own souls sincerely.

We are either genuine Christians or deceiving ourselves.

Unless Christ dwells within us through his Spirit and the power of his love, our claimed faith is dead and we remain unapproved by the One who will judge us.

Pray for holiness rather than merely escape from suffering (verses 7–10)

The greatest good we can pray for, both for ourselves and for those we love, is that we should not sin.

We have far more reason to pray to be preserved from doing evil than merely to be spared from suffering evil.

Paul wanted the Corinthians not only to turn away from wrongdoing, but also to grow in grace and holiness.

When we warn other people, we should also pray earnestly that they may stop doing wrong and learn to do what is good.

We should gladly see others become strong in Christ's grace, even if their growth reveals our own weakness.

And we should ask God to enable us to use every ability and opportunity he has entrusted to us.

Final encouragement and blessing (verses 11–14)

Paul ended his letter with several valuable exhortations.

God is the Author of peace and Lover of harmony.

He loves his people and is willing to live at peace with them.

We should therefore seek to live in such a way that separation from believing friends is only temporary.

We long to meet again in the world where parting will be unknown.

Paul's blessing asks that believers receive every benefit made available through the free grace and favor of Jesus Christ, purposed by the Father's free love, and applied and given by the Holy Spirit.

What a fitting conclusion to a letter containing both stern warnings and tender pastoral care!
classic_reading:
[2Cor.13.1-2Cor.13.6]
Chapter 13
Chapter Outline
The apostle threatens obstinate offenders. | (1-6) |
He prays for their reformation. | (7-10) |
And ends the epistle with a salutation and blessing. | (11-14) |
Verses 1-6
Though it is God's gracious method to bear long with sinners, yet he will not bear always; at length he will come, and will not spare those who remain obstinate and impenitent. Christ at his crucifixion, appeared as only a weak and helpless man, but his resurrection and life showed his Divine power. So the apostles, how mean and contemptible soever they appeared to the world, yet, as instruments, they manifested the power of God. Let them prove their tempers, conduct, and experience, as gold is assayed or proved by the touchstone. If they could prove themselves not to be reprobates, not to be rejected of Christ, he trusted they would know that he was not a reprobate, not disowned by Christ. They ought to know if Christ Jesus was in them, by the influences, graces, and indwelling of his Spirit, by his kingdom set up in their hearts. Let us question our own souls; either we are true Christians, or we are deceivers. Unless Christ be in us by his Spirit, and power of his love, our faith is dead, and we are yet disapproved by our Judge.
[2Cor.13.7-2Cor.13.10]
Verses 7-10
The most desirable thing we can ask of God, for ourselves and our friends, is to be kept from sin, that we and they may not do evil. We have far more need to pray that we may not do evil, than that we may not suffer evil. The apostle not only desired that they might be kept from sin, but also that they might grow in grace, and increase in holiness. We are earnestly to pray to God for those we caution, that they may cease to do evil, and learn to do well; and we should be glad for others to be strong in the grace of Christ, though it may be the means of showing our own weakness. let us also pray that we may be enabled to make a proper use of all our talents.
[2Cor.13.11-2Cor.13.14]
Verses 11-14
Here are several good exhortations. God is the Author of peace and Lover of concord; he hath loved us, and is willing to be at peace with us. And let it be our constant aim so to walk, that separation from our friends may be only for a time, and that we may meet in that happy world where parting will be unknown. He wishes that they may partake all the benefits which Christ of his free grace and favour has purchased; the Father out of his free love has purposed; and the Holy Ghost applies and bestows.
